summary:
Our team, The Eclipse, developed Selene Vector, a browser-based 3D game for the 2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge. Players design an uncrewed spacecraft, launch from Earth, plan orbital burns, and manage power on the way to the Moon. In lunar orbit, they use elevation and slope derived from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter data to choose a landing site. After touchdown, they collect and transmit simulated science data.

Selene Vector addresses the challenge by letting players make decisions across an entire space mission and see how those decisions affect the outcome. For example, carrying more propellant gives players more fuel for maneuvers but increases launch mass. Choosing a steeper landing site can cause a mission to fail even after a smooth descent. Replays and side-by-side mission comparisons let players test a different choice and see what changed. This makes NASA data and the engineering trade-offs behind lunar exploration accessible to students and anyone curious about spaceflight.
details:
What we developed

The Eclipse developed Selene Vector, a browser-based 3D game that lets players design and fly an uncrewed lunar science mission. Players choose a launcher, lander, fuel capacity, battery, and instruments. They then launch from Earth, plan orbital burns, correct their course, and manage battery power during an eclipse. After reaching lunar orbit, they select a landing target, fly a manual or assisted descent, and transmit simulated science observations back to Earth.

What makes it creative

The terrain map is part of the flight simulation. At Connecting Ridge near the lunar south pole, the same 5-meter elevation grid derived from NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter data shapes the 3D surface and determines ground contact and slope during touchdown. Players can compare a successful landing with a run that fails on steeper terrain, even when they descend gently in both attempts. Mission replays and side-by-side comparisons let them change one decision and see how it affects the outcome.

Tools and development

We used HTML and CSS for the interface, JavaScript for flight simulation and mission logic, and native WebGL for the 3D scenes. Python scripts processed NASA terrain data into the grid bundled with the game. Node.js handles local serving, builds, and automated tests. Players can run the standalone build offline on a computer with a WebGL-capable browser, without specialized hardware.

Benefits, intended impact, and design decisions

We designed Selene Vector for students, educators, and anyone curious about spaceflight. A classroom can compare two runs to explore how extra fuel affects launch mass, how an eclipse changes the power budget, or why terrain matters during touchdown. We considered how much detail a first-time player could use, where guidance would help, and which decisions should remain in the player’s hands. To keep missions playable, we simplified orbital dynamics and used fictional spacecraft and simulated science readings. We kept NASA’s terrain measurements distinct from the game’s touchdown rules so players can tell which information comes from the data and which limits were set for the simulation.
